basis.note: Written from the calculated result by fixed rules. No figure is added, rounded away or inferred; the technical result above is unchanged.

points: What this is: a test of whether daily coverage and a daily value from your dataset rise and fall together, at several time offsets.

What was found: the strongest pattern is at a lag of 2 days, with a rank correlation of 0.98 over 38 days. The chance of a pattern this strong across all lags tested, if there were no real link, is 0.001.

How it was found: ranks were compared at each offset, and chance was judged by shifting the data in time 999 times (keeping each series' day-to-day persistence), correcting for having looked at many offsets.
explanation.summary: Coverage tended to come before the change in your data.

terms.meaning: How many days coverage came before (positive) or after (negative) the change in your data.
The data is shifted around in time many times to see how often a pattern this strong appears by chance, while keeping each series' day-to-day persistence.

explanation.title: Explanation

result.reading: When coverage is higher, the value tends to be higher 2 day(s) after the coverage (rank correlation +0.98, adjusted p 0.001, 38 days). Coverage came first, which is an ordering in time and nothing more.
what_would_help: Check whether the pattern repeats in a period that was not used here.
Look for a known event that could drive both series.
Compare with a similar dataset or region that had no such coverage.
why_not_causal: A pattern in time does not show that one thing changed the other.
Something else (a season, a holiday, an event both react to) can move both series.
Coverage depends on which feeds were collected and when they were fetched.
